details: Noble gas source discrimination methodology: CTBTO four xenon isotopes monitored: Xe-133 (t½=5.24d); Xe-135 (t½=9.14hr); Xe-131m (t½=11.8d); Xe-133m (t½=2.19d); nuclear explosion discrimination ratios (time-corrected to same reference time): FRESH EXPLOSION (0-24hr after): Xe-135/Xe-133 = 3-10 (Xe-135 dominates because t½ short → fresh; fission yield ratios); AGED EXPLOSION (>7d): Xe-133/Xe-131m = 0.5-2 (Xe-133 → Xe-133m equilibrium); REACTOR ACCIDENT: Xe-133 from decay of I-133 (t½=20.8hr) → Xe-133 builds up over days; Xe-135 lower relative (burned in by 2.65×10⁶ barn resonance absorption in reactor before release); ratio: Xe-133/Xe-135 >> 3 = reactor signature; Kr-85 alone: civilian nuclear activities (fuel reprocessing; reactor venting); very specific; CTBTO standard: three-parameter discrimination: (1) Xe-133/Xe-135; (2) Xe-131m/Xe-133; (3) Transport time from source; achieves >95% discrimination accuracy for military vs civilian nuclear events
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl noble gas source term (1986): dominated by Xe-133 (4700 PBq; t½=5.24d); Xe-135 (released primarily first 24hr; then decayed; t½=9.14hr; shorter than Chernobyl release duration); if Chernobyl occurred today: CTBTO would classify as: (1) NOT nuclear explosion (Xe-133/Xe-135 >> 3 after Day 1); (2) REACTOR ACCIDENT (Xe-133 buildup over 14 days consistent with fission product decay chain); (3) Civilian nuclear: sustained multi-day noble gas release = reactor fire not explosion test; this discrimination in 2026: would occur within 24-48hr; public communication: 'reactor accident confirmed; not military nuclear test' = important public safety message (prevents nuclear weapon speculation)

details: Forsmark NPP detection of Chernobyl plume (historical): April 28 1986; Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant; Uppsala County; Sweden; time: approximately 07:00 (Central European Summer Time); event: radiation alarm triggered at Forsmark security checkpoint; worker returning from outdoor area found contaminated shoes; Forsmark immediate response: plant emergency procedure → search for internal leak; all workers screened → 90 workers with contamination; searches within plant found NO internal source; CONCLUSION: external contamination event; Swedish Radiation Authority (SSI) contacted; Swedish meteorologists: checked atmospheric backtrack trajectories → identified Soviet Union as likely source; Swedish Foreign Ministry contacted Soviet embassy; Soviet response: initially denied; April 28 14:00 local time: TASS announcement (66hr after accident); Sweden was the nation that forced Soviet disclosure by demonstrating: (1) Independent detection; (2) Atmospheric trajectory pointing to USSR; (3) Diplomatic pressure impossible to deflect
